summary:
Berry opens by defining GTM engineering as removing the constraints that historically prevented go-to-market teams from shipping at product-team speed, noting the role's recent explosion as an index on AI advances. He then surveys four hard technical areas.

First, data. The goal is a perfect virtual copy of the market, but accounts are in constant flux due to acquisitions, office openings, product launches, hiring/firing, and the GTM team's own activities. Because vendors never have a complete picture, teams use waterfalling—layering providers like Forager to fill gaps, with phone-number coverage from a single provider illustrating roughly half coverage. Either the user or the vendor must run evals. First-party data must also be kept current, but full refresh is expensive when data is purchased, so teams selectively choose fields to update. Different third-party representations of the same account also require entity resolution.

Second, orchestration. With 20–30 tools in a typical stack—CRM, warehouse, sequencer, dialer, note-taker, chat—each system has different needs: some want real-time single-record updates, others hundreds of thousands nightly; employee count changes constantly while headquarters rarely does. Hidden CRM-to-sequencer syncs force waits, weights, and loops to confirm readiness. Clay's solution is a graph of general-purpose nodes: agents, tool calls, conditionals, code, and a map-reduce fan-out triggered by events or schedules.

Third, agents. GTM needs long-running, per-account, mostly dormant agents spanning weeks or months of deal cycles. They wake via smart triggers or heartbeats, ingest current account context, support human feedback, and pursue continual learning for next-best-action. Berry recommends separating agent-updated fields from deterministic-system and human-updated fields, and shows a closed-lost reawaken agent that pulls from Gong, email, CRM, and the warehouse on a delay before re-engaging an account.

Fourth, execution. Cold email reply rates are low (roughly 0.5–1% across ~20M Smart Lead emails), so agentic execution must protect thin margins. Human-constraint problems include deciding whether to send as the rep versus the agent, using multiple domains to protect domain reputation, and routing replies back to the main domain. Multi-channel outreach adds suppression problems—e.g., canceling email sequences when a call connects and books a meeting, or unenrolling from lifecycle campaigns—making cross-channel coordination another agent-worthy problem.

In Q&A, Berry identifies the human-to-agent interface as one of the hardest unsolved problems, since reps must understand what agents did before joint calls with prospects. He confirms GTM engineering applies to inbound as well, citing routing, qualification, and historical-context handling.

sections.title: Intro: What GTM engineering is and why it exploded
sections.summary: Berry defines GTM engineering as removing constraints so GTM teams ship at product-team cadence, citing Clay's 2-week push cycle. He frames the role's recent growth as an index on AI advances and previews a four-area breakdown.

sections.title: Data: building a perfect virtual copy of the market
sections.summary: The data goal is a perfect virtual copy of the market, but accounts are in constant flux. Berry walks through a Clay CRM view, then introduces waterfalling across hundreds of vendors—using Forager's ~50% phone-number coverage as an example—and the need for evals.

sections.title: Data refresh, first-party signals, and entity resolution
sections.summary: Beyond third-party data, teams must incorporate first-party signals. Because purchased data refresh is expensive, teams selectively pick which fields to update. Multiple third-party representations of one account require entity resolution to support automated GTM plays.

sections.title: Orchestration across 20–30 tools with different refresh needs
sections.summary: Orchestration keeps a 10–30 tool stack in sync. Systems vary widely: some need real-time single-record updates, others hundreds of thousands nightly, with employee count changing constantly and headquarters rarely. Failures are constant, making this a complex data engineering problem.

sections.title: Hidden CRM-to-sequencer syncs and waits
sections.summary: Tools sync to each other behind the user's back; contacts created in a CRM must propagate to a sequencer before action. Berry introduces weights and loops to check readiness, motivating Clay's graph-based orchestration model.

sections.title: Clay's graph of general-purpose orchestration nodes
sections.summary: Clay uses a graph of general-purpose nodes: agents, tool calls, conditionals, code, and a map-reduce fan-out. A walkthrough shows a trigger or schedule, calls to multiple systems, a combine step, and pushes to rep interfaces.

sections.title: Agents: long-running, per-account, high-stakes
sections.summary: After data and orchestration, the system becomes complex with signals, data updates, agent/rep actions, meetings, and feedback. Agents now handle this context but share LLM problems. GTM needs very long-running, per-account agents across weeks or months, with a high error bar and mapping from unstructured agent output into structured systems like CRMs. The section ends mid-architecture description.

sections.title: Agent architecture: dormancy, triggers, feedback, and continual learning
sections.summary: Berry completes the agent picture: each account has a persistent, mostly dormant agent woken by smart triggers or heartbeats, which then ingests current context from data and orchestration layers and supports human feedback. The cutting edge is a learning phase where the agent updates its own view of what works; continual learning and next-best-action suggestions remain open problems.

sections.title: Basic and closed-lost reawaken agent examples
sections.summary: Berry shows a basic agent pulling from multiple sources with reasoning steps and updating agent-only CRM fields, recommending separation from deterministic and human fields. He then walks through a closed-lost reawaken agent that pulls from Gong, email, CRM, and the warehouse on a time-based trigger before re-engaging an account, highlighting timing and context issues.

sections.title: Execution: human constraints, domain reputation, and multi-channel coordination
sections.summary: With data, orchestration, and agents in place, execution is the hardest part. Cold email reply rates sit at roughly 0.5–1% across ~20M Smart Lead emails, so agentic mistakes compound on thin margins. Berry outlines human-constraint problems: rep-proxied vs. agent sending, multi-domain sending to protect domain reputation, reply routing back to the main domain, and multi-channel suppression such as canceling email sequences when a call connects. He shows a rep-proxied setup with rep inboxes connected to a sequencer.

sections.title: Closing and Q&A: the human-agent interface
sections.summary: Berry closes by urging teams to design around the harder constraints rather than overlook them. In Q&A he names the human-agent interface—where reps may not know what agents did—as one of the hardest problems, especially since humans still take joint calls with prospects. He also clarifies that GTM engineering covers inbound, including routing, qualification, and historical context handling.

organization.name: Clay
organization.summary: Clay is an independent go-to-market company that builds infrastructure for GTM engineers: get any data, run agentic workflows, and launch GTM plays. First-party pages describe a data marketplace of 200+ providers with waterfall enrichment, Claygents and Account Agents, orchestration workflows, and execution tools including a native sequencer. The about page says Clay makes creative tools for growth teams and that a single person can run campaigns that previously required a full GTM team; it also reports a January 2026 tender at a $5B valuation after a 2025 Series C at $3.1B. Everett Berry is Head of GTM Engineering at Clay and titled speaker; the talk uses Clay CRM views and everett@clay.com. retttx.com is his personal site, not the implementation owner.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. Homepage, about page, and university.clay.com/docs are live. About page states 500,000+ GTM teams, a Chelsea NYC office, and backing from Sequoia and others. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
